013 - Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth: Superman, Batman, and Spider-Man began as comic-book characters in the 1930s and 1960s and have since become worldwide icons through blockbuster films. Superhero comics, an original American art form like jazz, work as modern myths that dramatize philosophy's deepest questions: what makes someone a hero, whether an invulnerable being can risk anything, when crime-fighting becomes vigilantism, and how selflessness relates to self-interest. Philosophers and comic-book writers tackle them together, from Plato and Aristotle to Watchmen's question of who watches the watchmen.
014 - The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - C: The Atkins Diet is the low-carbohydrate regimen first popularized by Dr. Robert Atkins in the 1970s, which tells dieters to skip bread and sugar and eat meat and fat instead, defying mainstream nutrition advice while selling millions of books. Precisely because it flouts expert consensus, it raises genuine philosophical puzzles: how should a rational person decide what to eat, what to believe, and whom to believe? Essays draw on Kant, Hume, Nietzsche, and Dewey to examine habit, autonomy, low-carb nostalgia for a hunter-gatherer past, and the quality of the evidence in diet books.
015 - The Chronicles of Narnia and Philo: The Chronicles of Narnia is C.S. Lewis's beloved seven-book fantasy series (1950-1956), in which English children pass through a wardrobe and other doorways into a magical land ruled by the lion Aslan. Lewis taught philosophy at Oxford before becoming Christianity's best-known modern apologist, and his stories quietly stage serious questions: when should you believe incredible testimony, what may be accepted on faith, could more than one religion be true, and could a boy turned into a dragon remain the same person? Philosophers work through them with epistemology, Hume, Kierkegaard, and Pascal.
016 - Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 R: Hip-hop is the culture born in the 1970s Bronx - rapping, DJing, breakdancing, and graffiti - now a dominant force in popular music worldwide. This book takes seriously hip-hop's self-declared but often suppressed fifth element, knowledge, treating MCs like Rakim, Lauryn Hill, Jay-Z, Tupac, and Ice Cube as thinkers who probe God, love, authenticity, punishment, capitalism, and racial injustice. Like Socrates, the argument goes, the rap battle and frank street speech are cross-examination - philosophy done outside the academy.
017 - Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Al: Bob Dylan, the American singer-songwriter who reshaped popular music from the 1960s onward and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016, has written songs of protest, love, faith, and disillusion for six decades. His dense, allusive lyrics reward philosophical reading: essays trace an arc from Plato's ladder of love to Kierkegaardian despair, ask whether a racist killer is culpable or a 'pawn' manufactured by white supremacy, weigh the ethics of bootleg recordings, and test his protest politics against Kant's enlightenment and postmodern skepticism.
018 - Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - F: Harley-Davidson, the American motorcycle maker founded in 1903, builds the heavy, rumbling bikes that became icons of freedom and rebellion - Marlon Brando, Easy Rider, leather and bandanas. For riders a Harley is less a machine than a decision about how to live, which is exactly why it invites philosophy: essays use Pirsig's Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance, Heidegger on authentic existence, the Hellenistic schools of ancient Greece, and Hegel and Marx to ask what the ride means, why bikers form an instant brotherhood, and how commerce corrodes it.
019 - Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudg: Monty Python was the British comedy troupe whose 1969-74 television show and films like Life of Brian and The Meaning of Life made surreal absurdity a pillar of popular comedy. The connection to philosophy is literal: several Pythons absorbed the linguistic analysis of Wittgenstein, Russell, and Ryle at Oxford and Cambridge in the 1960s. Essays use the Dead Parrot sketch to test theories of meaning, the Argument Clinic to illustrate Rawls, and Mr. Creosote to explain why we laugh at the monstrous - and ask whether comedy can answer life's absurdity.
020 - Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rock: Poker is the card game of betting and bluffing, and no-limit Texas Hold'em - the version played at the World Series of Poker - has made professionals like Doyle Brunson and Chris Ferguson celebrities, especially after television and the 2003 internet-qualifier boom. The game is a natural philosophy laboratory: every hand forces decisions under uncertainty, incomplete knowledge of other minds, and genuine risk. Essays weigh bluffing against Kantian honesty, read the all-in bet through Kierkegaard's leap of faith, and ask whether Dostoevsky was right that gambling exposes the limits of reason.
021 - U2 and Philosophy - How to Deciphe: U2 is the Irish rock band - Bono, the Edge, Adam Clayton, and Larry Mullen Jr. - that rose from late-1970s Dublin post-punk to become one of the world's biggest bands, with The Joshua Tree among rock's landmark albums. Their songs wrestle publicly with faith, love, fame, technology, and global suffering, which makes them fertile philosophical ground: essays read their longing songs through Plato's ladder of love, Bono's stage personas through Kierkegaard and Baudrillard, and the band's desert imagery through Heidegger on place and belonging.
022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicke: Vampires and zombies are the Undead of popular horror - from Dracula and George Romero's zombie films to Twilight, True Blood, and Shaun of the Dead - and the twenty-first century has made them more popular than ever. They are also perfect thought experiments: is becoming a vampire worse than dying, does a zombie remain the person it used to be, and why do we kill zombies without qualms? Essays deploy Locke, Hume, Nietzsche, and the replicants of Blade Runner to interrogate personal identity, the badness of death, rights, and other minds.
